1.title: CT Abdomen — Renal Stone Protocol
1.contrast_note: Unenhanced low-dose stone protocol; no IV contrast is given. Calculi, calcifications, hydronephrosis/hydroureter and secondary obstruction signs (perinephric stranding, tissue-rim sign) are conspicuous; enhancement-dependent diagnoses — solid-tumour vascularity, active haemorrhage, acute pyelonephritis, and mural cystitis — are occult and must not be asserted on enhancement grounds. Bladder-wall thickening alone is non-specific and is NOT enhancement-characterisable here, so Cystitis is kept but flagged occult (not dropped), mirroring how the non-contrast study 4 treats Acute pyelonephritis.
hints: Classic target: obstructing ureteric calculus with secondary signs — report phrasings 'calculus at the VUJ/PUJ', 'proximal hydroureteronephrosis', 'perinephric fat stranding', 'soft-tissue/tissue-rim sign'.

Staghorn calculus fills the renal pelvis and calyces (branching, mould-like); pyelolithiasis = pelvicalyceal stone; a non-obstructing calyceal/renal stone maps to the canonical Urolithiasis leaf (do not invent a synonym leaf).
Pitfall — phlebolith vs distal ureteric calculus: phleboliths are rounded, may show a lucent centre / comet-tail and lie below the ischial spine; do not label them Ureteric calculus.
Pitfall — do NOT over-call Small renal mass / Primary renal neoplasia on unenhanced imaging; an indeterminate soft-tissue density is not a tumour without contrast.
Milk of calcium in a calyceal diverticulum and hyperdense (haemorrhagic/proteinaceous) renal cyst mimic stones — layering dependent calcium and >20 HU homogeneous cyst respectively.
Medullary nephrocalcinosis (medullary sponge kidney) vs cortical nephrocalcinosis — preserve the medullary/cortical location in the quote.

Cystitis is enhancement-limited but still reportable: if the report states 'bladder wall thickening ± cystitis', map it to the Cystitis leaf rather than the generic other bucket — non-specific is not unreportable.
Emergent second-look: high-grade obstruction (Obstructive uropathy, marked Hydronephrosis) with forniceal rupture, and any pneumatosis — bowel-wall gas is an ischaemia flag even on a stone study.

2.title: CT Abdomen/Pelvis — IV Contrast
2.contrast_note: Single-phase IV contrast (typically portal-venous). Solid-organ lesions, bowel mural hyperenhancement, abscess/collections, active luminal extravasation, lymphadenopathy and venous/arterial pathology are conspicuous; true dynamic characterisation is NOT available — LI-RADS arterial hyperenhancement + washout cannot be applied, so do not assert Hepatocellular carcinoma on dynamic criteria and treat hypervascular-lesion calls cautiously.
hints: High-yield acute abdomen: appendicitis, colonic diverticulitis, bowel obstruction (find the transition point), mesenteric ischaemia, perforation — report phrasings 'fat stranding', 'wall thickening with mural hyperenhancement', 'free fluid', 'free air', 'dilated fluid-filled loops'.

Solid-organ on portal-venous: hepatic metastases (hypodense), haemangioma (peripheral nodular discontinuous fill-in), simple cyst; renal cell carcinoma (enhancing mass >20 HU); adrenal adenoma (low HU) vs metastasis.
Vascular/emergent: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm ± Endoleak, splenic/portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, iliofemoral DVT; intraluminal contrast blush = active GI bleed.
Pitfall — do NOT call HCC from a single phase; Transient hepatic attenuation differences and Hepatic pseudolesions are over-called as tumour.
Pitfall — Pneumatosis intestinalis vs benign intraluminal gas; mesenteric ischaemia is a secondary-sign diagnosis (bowel-wall changes, mesenteric vessel occlusion, pneumatosis, portal venous gas).
Pitfall — Hypervascular metastases (NET, RCC, melanoma) need arterial phase and may be occult here; note their absence is not exclusion.

Emergent leaves to re-check in Pass 3 are listed under second_look — perforation (Pathological gas / Postoperative pneumoperitoneum), obstruction, ischaemia, pancreatic/biliary necrosis, aortic and haemorrhagic diagnoses.

3.title: CT Abdomen/Pelvis — Multiphase
3.contrast_note: Multiphase IV contrast (arterial + portal-venous ± delayed). Enables dynamic characterisation — LI-RADS arterial-phase hyperenhancement with washout ± enhancing capsule (Hepatocellular carcinoma / LR-5), hypervascular metastases, and renal enhancement/wash-in are callable; active arterial extravasation and pseudoaneurysm are conspicuous on the arterial phase. Formal adrenal-adenoma washout requires a dedicated adrenal washout protocol (unenhanced + 60s + 15-min delayed with absolute/relative washout) and should NOT be asserted on this generic multiphase study.
hints: LI-RADS in the cirrhotic liver: HCC = arterial hyperenhancement (APHE) + portal/delayed washout ± enhancing capsule — report phrasings 'APHE', 'washout', 'pseudocapsule', 'LR-5'; grade uncertain nodules as uncertain, not asserted.
Hypervascular lesions: FNH (central scar, near-isodense on delayed), haemangioma (peripheral nodular discontinuous progressive fill-in), hypervascular metastases (neuroendocrine, RCC, melanoma).
Renal-mass work-up: RCC enhances (>20 HU wash-in) — distinguish from hyperdense/haemorrhagic cyst which does not enhance.
Pancreas: hypoenhancing ductal adenocarcinoma vs pancreatitis; arterial phase defines vascular encasement and pseudoaneurysm.
Vascular emergent: pseudoaneurysm, visceral/splenic artery aneurysm, active contrast blush, aortic pathology, endoleak.

Pitfall — Transient hepatic attenuation differences and Hepatic pseudolesions (e.g. near the falciform ligament) mimic hypervascular tumour on the arterial phase; do not over-call Hypervascular liver lesions.

Pass-3 second-look targets the emergent leaves listed — this is the classic active-bleed / vascular-emergency protocol, so do not let lesion-characterisation focus mask GI bleeding, strangulating obstruction, ischaemia, haemorrhage, aortic or biliary emergencies.

4.title: CT Abdomen/Pelvis — Non-Contrast
4.contrast_note: Unenhanced (no IV contrast). Calcifications, stones, macroscopic fat, gas (pneumoperitoneum, pneumatosis, portal venous gas), acute/hyperdense haemorrhage, aortic intramural haematoma and bony lesions are conspicuous; enhancement-dependent diagnoses — solid-tumour vascularity, active extravasation, abscess-vs-phlegmon, bowel mural hyperenhancement, acute pyelonephritis, mural cystitis — are occult and must not be asserted on enhancement grounds (they are kept but flagged occult, not dropped).
hints: Non-contrast strengths: urolithiasis, acute haematoma (hyperdense clot), aortic intramural haematoma (crescentic high-density wall), fat-containing lesions (angiomyolipoma, adrenal myelolipoma, lipoma), bony metastases/fractures, free air and pneumatosis.

Emergent, all callable unenhanced: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm ± Spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage, Aortic intramural haematoma, Pathological gas / pneumoperitoneum, Pneumatosis intestinalis, bowel obstruction.

Report phrasings that flag the unenhanced setting: 'no IV contrast administered', 'hyperdense', 'calcified', 'fat density / negative HU'; perinephric fat stranding is the key secondary sign of obstruction/haemorrhage.
Pitfall — cannot characterise enhancing masses: an indeterminate soft-tissue density is not a tumour; do not assert Renal cell carcinoma or hypervascular lesions on unenhanced images.
Pitfall — bowel-wall thickening without enhancement data is nonspecific; do not confidently call ischaemic or infectious colitis.
Fat-containing adrenal lesion = myelolipoma / lipid-rich adenoma (macroscopic or low HU) — well seen unenhanced.

5.title: CT Cervical Spine
5.contrast_note: Routine CT cervical spine is non-contrast: osseous detail (fractures, degenerative/ossific disease, sclerotic vs lytic lesions) and the craniocervical junction are exquisitely seen, and lower-neck soft tissues (thyroid) fall in the field of view. Cord, discs, ligaments, marrow-replacing tumour and epidural/subdural collections are only inferred — do not label enhancement-based diagnoses; hedge cord/soft-tissue calls that truly need MRI. Acute spinal epidural/subdural haematoma is largely an MRI/active-bleed diagnosis: label 'Extradural and Subdural Haematoma' ONLY when the report itself explicitly asserts it (default to uncertain on non-contrast CT).
hints: Degenerative disease is bread-and-butter: Spondylosis, Osteophyte, uncovertebral/Facet joint arthropathy, Intervertebral osteochondrosis, Cervical foraminal stenosis; OPLL/OLF (Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament / ligamentum flavum) narrow the canal — reported as 'ossified PLL causing canal stenosis'.

Trauma phrasings: 'fracture through', 'cortical disruption/step-off', dens/odontoid, C1 ring — a Jefferson fracture is a TRAUMATIC C1 ring burst (map to Burst fracture / Cervical spine fractures), hangman fracture; prevertebral soft-tissue swelling is an indirect injury sign.

CONGENITAL CCJ mimics (non-traumatic): Split atlas (bipartite/median-cleft atlas) and Congenital anomalies of the posterior atlas arch are classic Jefferson-fracture mimics; Os odontoideum mimics a dens fracture — these have smooth corticated margins and must NOT be coded as a fracture unless the report describes acute cortical disruption. Also Occipital vertebra / Atlanto-occipital assimilation at this junction.

CRITICAL, easily missed: a transverse Chalk stick fracture through an ankylosed spine (DISH / ankylosing spondylitis) is highly unstable — scrutinise the whole ankylosed segment even on a limited study.
Craniocervical junction disease: Basilar invagination / Basilar skull fracture / Retro-odontoid pseudotumour (chronic atlantoaxial instability) — preserve the anatomic level in the quote.
Vertebral haemangioma = classic 'corduroy'/'polka-dot' benign lesion; only the Aggressive variant shows cortical breach/extraosseous soft tissue — do not up-code a bland haemangioma.
Pitfall — do not over-call sclerotic metastasis: a Bone island (enostosis) is a benign well-marginated dense focus; Vacuum phenomenon (disc/facet gas) is degenerative, not infective gas.
Incidental neck soft tissue in FOV: Thyroid nodule / Multinodular goitre / Thyroid carcinoma — label only if the report states them.

6.title: CT Chest — IV Contrast
6.contrast_note: Single-phase venous-timed IV-contrast chest (portal/late-venous). Mediastinal/hilar nodes, pleural and pericardial disease, and nodal/soft-tissue enhancement are conspicuous; not ECG-gated and venous-timed, so call only large/central PE (not subsegmental clot) and treat fine coronary/leaflet detail as unreliable.
hints: Lung nodules/masses are high-yield: distinguish 'solitary pulmonary nodule', 'part-solid lung nodule', 'ground-glass nodule', and frank 'Pulmonary mass'/'Lung cancer'. Pitfall — do not upgrade multiple small nodules to 'Pulmonary metastases' unless the report says metastatic.

Mediastinal/hilar nodes are the strength of this study: 'Mediastinal lymphadenopathy', 'Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy', 'Right paratracheal lymphadenopathy' — short-axis >1 cm; low-attenuation/necrotic nodes suggest TB or metastasis; bulky nodal disease raises 'Non-Hodgkin lymphoma'.
Pleural fluid — grade it: bland 'Pleural effusion' vs 'Parapneumonic effusion' vs loculated enhancing 'Empyema'; enhancing nodular pleura → 'Malignant pleural disease'/'Pleural metastases'.

Airway/parenchymal chronic disease is common: 'Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease', 'Centrilobular pulmonary emphysema', 'Bronchiectasis', interstitial patterns ('Honeycombing', 'Usual Interstitial Pneumonia', 'Interstitial lung disease').

Consolidation vs collapse: 'Consolidation'/'Lobar pneumonia' vs 'Lung atelectasis'/lobar-collapse leaves. Pitfall — dependent 'Gravity-dependent atelectasis' is routinely over-called as consolidation.
Aorta and great vessels: report 'Thoracic aortic dilatation'/'Thoracic aortic aneurysm'/'Ascending aortic aneurysm'; contrast makes 'Aortic dissection' and 'Aortic intramural haematoma' callable.
Common report phrasings: 'spiculated', 'necrotic node', 'loculated effusion with enhancing pleura', 'saccular aneurysm', 'intimal flap'.

7.title: CT Chest — Non-Contrast / HRCT / LDCT
7.contrast_note: Non-contrast acquisition — HRCT for diffuse/interstitial lung disease, LDCT for screening. No IV enhancement: do NOT label enhancement- or perfusion-dependent diagnoses (pulmonary embolism, active extravasation, vessel-wall/nodal enhancement, aortic dissection intimal flap); vessels and nodes are assessed by size and calcification only. HRCT is optimal for interstitial pattern, air-trapping, bronchiectasis and emphysema.
hints: Interstitial pattern is the core task: map wording to pattern leaves — 'reticulation'/'traction bronchiectasis'/'Honeycombing'/subpleural basal → 'Usual Interstitial Pneumonia'/'Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis'; ground-glass with reticulation → 'Interstitial lung disease'. Pitfall — do not assert 'Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis' unless a UIP pattern or IPF is explicitly stated.

Emphysema subtype matters: 'Centrilobular pulmonary emphysema' (upper-zone, smokers), 'Paraseptal emphysema' (subpleural), 'Panlobular emphysema' (lower-zone, alpha-1); 'Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema' when both coexist.

Nodule characterisation for LDCT screening: 'Solitary pulmonary nodule', 'Part-solid lung nodule', 'Pure ground glass nodule', 'Calcified pulmonary nodules' (benign). Pitfall — perifissural/'Intrapulmonary lymph nodes' over-called as concerning nodules.

Small-airways disease: 'Mosaic attenuation pattern', 'Air trapping' (expiratory), 'Bronchiolitis'/'Infectious bronchiolitis' (tree-in-bud). Pitfall — mosaic attenuation is frequently over-read; needs expiratory confirmation.
Infection/inflammation: 'Consolidation', 'Bronchopneumonia', 'COVID-19' (peripheral GGO), 'Pulmonary Tuberculosis' (upper-lobe cavitation, tree-in-bud).
Asbestos/pleural: 'Pleural plaque', 'Pleural calcification', 'Asbestos-related benign pleural disease'; 'Diffuse pleural thickening'/'Fibrothorax'.
Aorta on non-contrast: 'Thoracic aortic dilatation'/'aneurysm' by calibre; a hyperdense crescent = 'Aortic intramural haematoma' (the one acute aortic entity reliably seen unenhanced).
Common phrasings: 'subpleural reticulation', 'tree-in-bud', 'centrilobular nodules', 'mosaic attenuation', 'traction bronchiectasis'.

8.title: CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis — IV Contrast
8.contrast_note: Single-phase portal-venous IV contrast: solid-organ and bowel-wall enhancement, rim-enhancing abscess, nodal characterisation and active extravasation are reliable. NOT multiphase, so arterial-only hypervascular-lesion characterisation (LI-RADS AHE+washout, small hypervascular metastases) is unreliable, and central/large PE is visible but this is not a PE-optimised CTPA — do not over-call subsegmental PE.
hints: Portal-venous CAP is the oncology-staging and sepsis workhorse: think primary tumour plus hepatic, pulmonary, nodal, adrenal and osseous metastases and diffuse lymphadenopathy.
Hepatic metastases read as hypodense lesions on portal-venous phase; ubiquitous 'too small to characterise' hypodensities are usually benign — do not up-code to metastasis without supporting wording.

Bowel emergencies: wall thickening, obstruction with a transition point, diverticulitis, appendicitis; reduced/absent mural enhancement or pneumatosis signals ischaemia — emergent, second-look Ischaemic colitis / Pneumatosis intestinalis.
Acute abdomen calls: free intraperitoneal gas ('pathological gas'), perforation, and rim-enhancing/gas-containing abscess collections.

Thorax: central/large pulmonary embolism ('filling defect in the pulmonary artery') is visible on portal-venous timing but subsegmental PE is unreliable; also pleural effusion, consolidation, nodules, and inspect the aorta for dissection or intramural haematoma even though this is not a dedicated angiogram.

Active haemorrhage = a focus of contrast pooling within a haematoma or bowel lumen — distinct from a non-active post-traumatic/spontaneous haematoma and from injection-site 'Contrast media extravasation'.
Pitfall: incidental adrenal, renal and hepatic lesions are frequently over-called as metastases — keep polarity and uncertainty faithful to the report wording.

9.title: CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis — Multiphase
9.contrast_note: Multiphase (arterial + portal-venous ± delayed): hypervascular lesions are fully callable — LI-RADS arterial hyperenhancement with washout (HCC), FNH, flash-filling haemangioma, hypervascular metastases, THADs, visceral-artery aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm and active arterial extravasation / GI bleeding. Arterial phase also optimises aortic dissection, intramural haematoma and penetrating ulcer.
hints: Lesion-characterisation study — use combined arterial + venous behaviour. Classic HCC = arterial hyperenhancement with washout in a cirrhotic liver; FNH = arterial enhancement with a delayed central scar; flash-filling haemangioma fills avidly.
Hypervascular metastases (neuroendocrine, RCC, melanoma, thyroid) are conspicuous on arterial phase — report as 'hypervascular / arterially enhancing lesions'.
Active bleeding = a focus of contrast pooling that grows on the delayed phase; look for GI bleeding, pseudoaneurysm and visceral-artery aneurysm.
Pancreas: arterial phase best shows hypovascular adenocarcinoma and mass-forming pancreatitis; grade acute pancreatitis for necrotising change.
Inspect the aorta on arterial phase for dissection, intramural haematoma and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.
Pitfall: transient hepatic attenuation differences and perfusion pseudolesions are easily over-called as metastases — keep them uncertain unless the report commits.
Pitfall: arterially-enhancing pseudolesions near the falciform ligament / capsule are benign and should not be labelled tumour.

10.title: CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis — Non-Contrast
10.contrast_note: No IV contrast: do NOT call enhancement-dependent diagnoses (active bleeding/extravasation, rim-enhancing abscess, pulmonary embolism, dissection flap). Conspicuous: calcifications, urolithiasis, acute hyperdense haemorrhage/haematoma, aortic intramural haematoma (hyperdense mural crescent), fractures, emphysema, ILD and pulmonary nodules; solid-organ lesions are seen but cannot be characterised.
hints: Non-contrast CAP strengths: stones (renal/ureteric/bladder, staghorn), vascular and soft-tissue calcifications, acute haemorrhage (hyperdense blood/haematoma), fractures, and lung parenchyma (emphysema, fibrosis, nodules).
Aortic intramural haematoma = hyperdense crescent in the aortic wall — callable without contrast; a dissection flap generally is NOT, so do not label 'aortic dissection' here.
Low liver attenuation = hepatic steatosis; incidental low-density hepatic/renal/adrenal lesions cannot be characterised — leave uncertain rather than naming a tumour.
Acute abdomen visible without contrast: pneumoperitoneum ('pathological gas'), pneumatosis intestinalis, and high-grade bowel obstruction.
Appendicitis on non-contrast = distended appendix, appendicolith and periappendiceal fat stranding; collection gas is seen but rim enhancement is not.
Pitfall: do NOT assert enhancement-dependent diagnoses (active extravasation, pulmonary embolism, hypervascular lesions) — the acquisition physically cannot demonstrate them.

11.title: CT Extremity
11.contrast_note: CT Extremity is typically NON-CONTRAST, acquired for cortical/trabecular bone and fracture detail; without IV contrast do not call enhancement-based diagnoses (active bleed, abscess-vs-phlegmon distinction, tumour vascularity) — abscess/fluid collection are inferred from morphology and gas only. Arterial-phase vascular endpoints (limb ischaemia) are not assessable; heavy mural calcification may be noted incidentally but PAD grading needs a dedicated CTA.
hints: Fractures dominate: name the pattern and site — scaphoid, calcaneal, tibial plateau, radial head, trimalleolar, posterior malleolus, Die-punch, pubic ramus; report phrasing 'lucent fracture line', 'cortical breach', 'articular step-off', comminuted (butterfly/segmental) vs complete.

Pathological fracture = fracture THROUGH a lytic/permeative lesion — always look for an underlying bone lesion (metastasis, myeloma); phrasing 'fracture through a lucent lesion', 'no antecedent trauma'.

Tarsal coalition (talocalcaneal / calcaneonavicular): osseous or fibrous mid/hindfoot bridge — 'C-sign', 'talar beak', 'anteater nose'; distinguish osseous coalition (Synostosis/Bony Coalition) from fibrous.
Femoroacetabular impingement: cam = aspherical femoral head-neck (high alpha angle), pincer = acetabular over-coverage/retroversion — do not conflate the two morphologies.
Chronic osteomyelitis: sequestrum + involucrum + cortical destruction/sinus tract; do NOT upgrade nonspecific marrow sclerosis or a solitary erosion to active infection on CT alone.
Benign gas mimics: Vacuum phenomenon / intra-articular gas / intraosseous pneumatocyst are BENIGN — reserve infection calls for soft-tissue gas with a drainable collection.

Sclerotic-lesion pitfall: bone island (enostosis, brush border, no growth) vs solitary sclerotic metastasis — do not upgrade a classic bone island to metastasis; likewise osteopoikilosis vs blastic mets.
Retained foreign body / gunshot: report metal vs glass fragments, count, and track/trajectory; Metal foreign body and Glass foreign body are distinct leaves.

12.title: CT Head — IV Contrast
12.contrast_note: Contrast-enhanced head CT (post-IV, parenchymal phase): enhancing pathology is conspicuous — ring-enhancing abscess, dural-based meningioma, enhancing or haemorrhagic metastases, blood-brain-barrier breakdown, luxury perfusion and post-thrombectomy contrast staining are callable. It is NOT a non-contrast study (subtle acute parenchymal blood can be masked by or mimic enhancement) and NOT a CTA — do NOT infer luminal occlusion, stenosis or aneurysm from parenchymal-phase images alone; capture those luminal/aneurysm diagnoses only when they are explicitly stated in the report (e.g. carried over from a companion CTA/NCCT), not reasoned from the parenchymal-phase appearance.
hints: Ring/rim-enhancing lesion with central low attenuation: abscess vs necrotic metastasis vs high-grade tumour — phrasings 'ring enhancement', 'rim-enhancing', 'central necrosis'.
Dural-based extra-axial enhancing mass with CSF cleft or dural tail -> Meningothelial meningioma; distinguish from an intra-axial mass.
Enhancing lesion(s) at the grey-white junction with surrounding vasogenic oedema -> Intracranial metastases / Hyperattenuating cerebral metastases / Intracranial tumours.
Mass-effect cascade to track: Intracranial mass effect -> Subfalcine herniation -> Transtentorial herniation -> Obstructive hydrocephalus -> Raised intracranial pressure.
Post-thrombectomy hyperdensity that follows a vascular territory and resolves is Contrast staining, not new Intracranial haemorrhage — do not over-call haemorrhage.

Pitfall: normal venous/parenchymal enhancement and a Developmental Venous Anomaly (caput medusae, no nidus) get over-called as Brain arteriovenous malformation — a true AVM needs a nidus with feeders/draining vein.

Second-look the emergent parenchymal leaves even on a 'tumour' protocol: Intracranial/Subarachnoid/Subdural haemorrhage, Ischaemic stroke and Middle cerebral artery infarct, herniations. Only tag Large vessel occlusion, Middle cerebral artery occlusion or Ruptured saccular aneurysm if the report explicitly states them (this is not a CTA) — do not infer luminal occlusion or an aneurysm from parenchymal-phase enhancement.

13.title: CT Head — Non-Contrast
13.contrast_note: Non-contrast head CT — the workhorse for acute neuro. Hyperacute blood (SAH, intraparenchymal, subdural, extradural, contusion), fracture, mass effect, hydrocephalus and established infarct hypodensity are the callable core. With NO IV contrast, do NOT assert enhancement-dependent diagnoses — no ring-enhancing abscess characterisation, no metastatic 'enhancement', and no hyperperfusion call. (Contrast staining IS reportable on post-thrombectomy NCCT as retained intra-arterial contrast.)
hints: Acute blood is hyperdense: crescentic Subdural haemorrhage, lentiform Extradural, sulcal/cisternal Subarachnoid haemorrhage, rounded Intracerebral haemorrhage — age it by attenuation.

Hyperdense MCA or dot sign -> Large vessel / Middle cerebral artery occlusion; loss of grey-white differentiation, insular-ribbon loss, basal-ganglia hypodensity -> early Ischaemic stroke / Ischemic Stroke Infarct Core.
Mass-effect/herniation cascade: midline shift -> Subfalcine herniation, uncal/Transtentorial herniation, effaced basal cisterns -> Raised intracranial pressure.

Trauma: read bone windows — Skull fracture, Basilar skull fracture, Mandibular/Nasal/facial fractures, pneumocephalus, and Coup-contrecoup contusions (Cerebral haemorrhagic contusion / Coup-contrecoup injury).
Hydrocephalus: temporal-horn dilation and transependymal (periventricular) oedema -> Obstructive vs Communicating hydrocephalus.

Pitfall: physiologic calcification (Basal ganglia calcification, Fahr syndrome, Falx ossification, choroid/pineal calcification) mimics acute blood — check symmetry/location/attenuation before calling Intracerebral haemorrhage.
Second-look the emergent leaves: SAH, Intracerebral / Subdural / Extradural haemorrhage, haemorrhagic contusions, herniations, Large vessel occlusion, infarct core.

14.title: CT Liver — Four-Phase
14.contrast_note: Four-phase liver protocol (non-contrast, late-arterial, portal-venous, delayed): arterial hyperenhancement with portal-venous/delayed washout and a pseudocapsule make HCC and hypervascular lesions conspicuous, and haemangioma centripetal fill-in and FNH central-scar behaviour are assessable. Do not read active arterial extravasation into a non-CTA study.
hints: HCC: arterial-phase hyperenhancement WITH portal-venous or delayed washout ± enhancing 'pseudocapsule', usually on a cirrhotic background — the full LR-5 signature.

Haemangioma: peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in; small 'flash-filling' lesions enhance avidly on arterial phase and can mimic HCC — retention on delayed phase distinguishes.
FNH: homogeneous arterial enhancement, iso-/hypodense on delayed phase, with a central scar that is hypodense on arterial/portal-venous phases and shows delayed enhancement; no washout.
Hypervascular metastases (esp. neuroendocrine/NET): multiple arterially-enhancing lesions — look for a known primary; contrast with solitary FNH/adenoma.

Focal fatty sparing / focal steatosis: geographic non-mass-like low (or spared) attenuation in classic sites (gallbladder fossa, adjacent to falciform, porta) with vessels coursing undisturbed — commonly OVER-called as a lesion.
THAD / transient hepatic attenuation differences: wedge-shaped arterial-only enhancement that normalises on portal-venous phase — a perfusion phenomenon, not a mass.

Cirrhosis morphology (nodular contour, caudate hypertrophy, capsular retraction) plus cirrhosis-associated / regenerative / dysplastic nodules; report portal hypertension and portosystemic collaterals when present.
Pseudolesions near the falciform ligament / gallbladder fossa are perfusion artefacts — do not label as metastasis.

15.title: CT Lumbar Spine
15.contrast_note: Routine CT lumbar spine is non-contrast: fractures, degenerative disc/facet disease, pars defects, canal geometry and lytic/sclerotic bone lesions are well seen; sacrum and lower rectum sit in the FOV. Discs, nerve roots, thecal sac contents, marrow oedema and epidural collections need MRI — do not label enhancement-based diagnoses, and hedge soft-tissue/marrow calls.
hints: Degenerative bread-and-butter: Intervertebral disc herniation, Intervertebral osteochondrosis (vacuum disc + endplate sclerosis), Facet joint arthropathy, Spondylosis, Anterolisthesis, and canal/foraminal narrowing (Congenital lumbar spinal stenosis, Trefoil spinal canal, Subarticular zone stenosis).
A pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis) commonly underlies Anterolisthesis — report the pars defect explicitly (see add_leaves).

CRITICAL/infective, easily missed: Chronic osteomyelitis (pyogenic spondylodiscitis) and Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (Pott disease) — 'endplate destruction', 'disc-space loss', 'paravertebral collection'.
Kümmell disease = intravertebral vacuum cleft within a collapsed osteonecrotic vertebra — do NOT down-label it as ordinary benign Vacuum phenomenon or a simple compression fracture.
Vacuum phenomenon (disc/facet gas), Intraosseous gas / Intraosseous pneumatocyst are degenerative/benign gas — not infection.

Pitfall — do not over-call sclerotic metastasis: Bone island (enostosis) and Intraosseous lipoma are benign; classic corduroy Vertebral haemangioma is benign unless the Aggressive variant is described. Conversely, second-look for marrow-replacing Sclerotic / Vertebral metastases (pedicle sign) — do not miss them.
Sacroiliitis, Transitional vertebra (Bertolotti), Oppenheimer ossicle are high-yield lumbosacral calls; Megarectum is an incidental pelvic finding only if stated.

16.title: CT Neck — IV Contrast
16.contrast_note: IV-contrast soft-tissue neck CT: abscess rim enhancement, cystic/necrotic nodal change, extranodal spread, and tumour/salivary/thyroid lesion conspicuity are callable. This is not a CTA — grade only frank carotid/vertebral luminal narrowing or gross vascular anomaly; do NOT characterise plaque morphology, vulnerable plaque, or active arterial bleed.
hints: Deep-neck / peritonsillar abscess — 'rim-enhancing fluid collection', 'phlegmon with central low attenuation'; emergent for airway compromise.

Nodal disease of HNSCC — 'necrotic/cystic node', 'centrally low-attenuation node', extranodal extension = capsular breach / spiculated node margin / matting; distinguish a cystic necrotic node from a second branchial cleft cyst by patient age and level.
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma — enhancing mucosal/submucosal mass (tonsil, tongue base, larynx, hypopharynx); look for the primary when a necrotic level II node is present.

Cystic congenital masses by location — thyroglossal duct cyst (midline, infrahyoid, embedded in strap muscle), second branchial cleft cyst (level II, posterolateral to submandibular gland).
Thyroid nodule / multinodular goitre are common incidentals; note substernal/retrosternal extension.
Pitfall: do not over-call 'Cervical lymphadenopathy' for sub-centimetre reactive nodes — require size/necrosis/number criteria stated in the report.

17.title: CT Neck — Non-Contrast
17.contrast_note: Non-contrast neck CT: bone detail, calcifications (sialoliths, ingested bone/foreign body, tonsilloliths), sinus/mastoid opacification, and goitre bulk are conspicuous. Enhancement-dependent calls — abscess wall, nodal necrosis, tumour margins, extranodal extension, active bleed — are unreliable here; do not ASSERT them, keep uncertain unless the report itself states them explicitly.
hints: Trauma is the classic NC indication — mandibular fracture, nasal bone fracture, complex midfacial fracture, cervical spine fractures/injury and hyperextension injury; emergent.
Ingested bones / foreign body — 'hyperdense foreign body' in the pharynx/upper oesophagus; report location and any adjacent gas/perforation.
Sialolithiasis — calcified calculus in the submandibular (Wharton) duct or gland; well seen without contrast.
Aerodigestive/sinus infection markers — otomastoiditis with mastoid air-cell opacification, odontogenic sinusitis; note these are opacification/erosion calls, not enhancement calls.
Thyroid bulk — multinodular goitre and substernal goitre are conspicuous by mass effect / tracheal deviation even without contrast.
Pitfall: tonsillitis, parotitis, and peritonsillar abscess need contrast for confident diagnosis — on NC only asymmetric swelling is visible; keep uncertain unless the report is explicit.
Pitfall: do not assert soft-tissue abscess or nodal necrosis on a non-contrast study.

18.title: CT Sinus / Facial / Orbits
18.contrast_note: Typically NON-CONTRAST, read on bone and soft-tissue windows; exquisite for bony walls, air-fluid levels, mucosal thickening, ossification and foreign bodies. Do NOT label enhancement-dependent diagnoses (rim-enhancing abscess, active bleed, tumour vascularity) — soft-tissue mass characterisation is limited, so infiltrative/malignant lesions are inferred from bone destruction, not enhancement.
hints: Highest-yield: chronic rhinosinusitis, acute rhinosinusitis (air-fluid level), sinonasal polyposis, paranasal sinus retention cyst, deviated nasal septum — reported constantly; anchor each to the named sinus/side in the quote.
Odontogenic sinusitis: unilateral maxillary opacification with adjacent periapical/dental disease — look for the maxillary-molar link before calling it.

Fungal sinusitis: hyperattenuating/calcified sinus content ('hyperdense', 'hyperattenuating paranasal sinus opacification', 'inspissated secretions') — allergic fungal vs invasive; invasive fungal is emergent.

Orbital trauma phrasing: 'blow-out fracture', 'inferior/medial orbital wall fracture', 'lamina papyracea', with herniated fat/muscle, hypoglobus or proptosis — pair the fracture with any orbital-content sign.
Facial fracture families: 'naso-orbito-ethmoid', 'ZMC/tripod', 'Le Fort', 'complex midfacial' — map to the specific leaf, not the generic 'Facial fractures', when the pattern is named.

PITFALL — over-call: minimal mucosal thickening is NOT sinusitis; a smooth dome-shaped opacity is a retention cyst, not polyposis; a single osteoma should not be doubled as skull vault + paranasal osteoma.
Second-look the orbit and skull base: ocular/metal foreign body, globe/scleral calcification, and lytic skull lesions are easily missed on a 'sinus' read.

19.title: CT Temporal Bones
19.contrast_note: High-resolution NON-CONTRAST bone-algorithm study; exquisite for ossicles, otic capsule, scutum, mastoid air cells and canal/wall dehiscences. No contrast → do NOT characterise enhancing masses (paraganglioma, vestibular schwannoma, facial-nerve enhancement) or intracranial complications; soft-tissue opacity is adjudicated by BONY EROSION (cholesteatoma) vs its absence (effusion/granulation/tympanosclerosis), not enhancement.
hints: Chronic otomastoiditis is the workhorse call — 'mastoid/middle-ear opacification', 'soft tissue', with sub-calls for ossicular erosion and tympanosclerosis; grade by the associated bony change.
Cholesteatoma = soft tissue with SCUTUM blunting / ossicular or lateral-canal erosion; do NOT call cholesteatoma for opacification without erosion (that is granulation tissue or effusion).

Otosclerosis: fenestral lucency at the fissula ante fenestram is the classic form; retrofenestral (cochlear) otosclerosis is the pericochlear form — map both to the single 'Otosclerosis' leaf and do NOT double-label.

Third-window/variant phrasing: 'superior semicircular canal dehiscence', 'sigmoid sinus / jugular bulb dehiscence or diverticulum', 'high-riding jugular bulb' — map precisely; do not conflate high-riding with dehiscent.
Congenital: enlarged vestibular aqueduct, Mondini/incomplete-partition, external canal exostoses ('surfer's ear').
PITFALL — over-call: dehiscent/high jugular bulb and sigmoid diverticulum are frequently over-read; require the explicit report wording.
Second-look for trauma/aggression: temporal-bone/basilar skull fracture, haemotympanum, and lytic/metastatic skull lesion on a 'chronic ear' read.

20.title: CT Thoracic Spine
20.contrast_note: Routine CT thoracic spine is non-contrast: vertebral fractures, degenerative/ossific disease, alignment and lytic/sclerotic bone lesions are well seen, with paravertebral lung and mediastinum partly in the FOV. Cord, discs, marrow oedema and epidural collections need MRI — do not label enhancement-based or active-bleed diagnoses; hedge cord/soft-tissue calls.
hints: Osteoporotic vertebral compression / wedge fractures are very common thoracic findings — distinguish benign from Pathological/Vertebral body pathological fracture (posterior-wall bulge, pedicle destruction, paravertebral soft tissue).

CRITICAL, easily missed: a transverse Chalk stick (carrot-stick) fracture through an ankylosed DISH / ankylosing-spondylitis spine is grossly unstable — review the entire fused segment; second-look even on a limited study.

Metastatic disease favours the thoracic spine (#1 site): Lytic / Sclerotic / Mixed lytic and sclerotic bone metastases, Vertebral metastases, Spinal metastasis — the easily-missed 'pedicle sign' (absent pedicle / marrow-replacing lesion) is the key second-look target.
Kümmell disease = intravertebral vacuum cleft in a collapsed osteonecrotic vertebra — do not down-label as benign Vacuum phenomenon.
DISH = flowing anterior ossification bridging ≥4 contiguous levels; Ankylosing spondylitis = squaring/syndesmophytes/'bamboo spine'; both create the brittle ankylosed spine above.
Infective: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (Pott disease) — endplate destruction with paravertebral/psoas collection.
Pitfall — Bone island and classic corduroy Vertebral haemangioma are benign; reserve the Aggressive vertebral haemangioma label for cortical breach/soft-tissue extension.

21.title: CT Urography
21.contrast_note: Multiphase CT urography (non-contrast → nephrographic → excretory): non-contrast detects calculi/density and fat-containing AML, the nephrographic phase characterises enhancing renal masses, and the excretory phase opacifies the collecting system, ureters and bladder — making urothelial filling defects, obstruction level, forniceal rupture and duplication conspicuous.
hints: Urolithiasis / ureteric calculus: dense non-contrast focus with secondary hydroureteronephrosis, perinephric/periureteric stranding, ureteric wall oedema ('soft-tissue rim sign') and a delayed/persistent nephrogram on the obstructed side.

Urothelial carcinoma (bladder or upper tract): enhancing soft-tissue filling defect / focal urothelial thickening seen against opacified urine on the excretory phase — the reason urography is ordered; report bladder vs ureter/renal-pelvis location.
RCC / solid renal mass: enhancing (>20 HU) soft-tissue mass on the nephrographic phase; report small renal mass separately when sub-4 cm.
Angiomyolipoma: macroscopic fat within a renal mass on non-contrast/nephrographic images — do not label a fat-containing lesion as RCC.

Congenital / anatomic variants are high-yield here: duplex collecting system, horseshoe/ectopic/crossed-fused kidney, circumcaval (retrocaval) ureter, megaureter — read the excretory phase for collecting-system anatomy.

Pitfalls: milk-of-calcium or a calyceal diverticulum mimicking an obstructing stone; a parapelvic/renal-sinus cyst mimicking hydronephrosis (follow it onto the excretory phase); medullary sponge kidney's papillary 'paintbrush' opacification vs nephrocalcinosis.
Forniceal rupture: perinephric contrast extravasation on the excretory phase in a high-grade obstruction — an emergent finding.

22.title: CTA Abdomen
22.contrast_note: Arterial-phase abdominal CTA: intimal flaps, true/false lumina, intramural haematoma, aneurysm calibre, penetrating ulcer, endoleak, pseudoaneurysm, active arterial extravasation and visceral/renal/iliac branch stenosis/occlusion are directly callable. Venous structures are sub-optimally opacified — do not deny venous thrombosis on this phase, and read asserted venous findings as report-stated.
hints: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: infrarenal aortic dilatation ≥3 cm; flag rupture/impending-rupture signs (peri-aortic/retroperitoneal haematoma, 'draped aorta', hyperdense crescent) — an emergency.

Aortic dissection: intimal flap dividing true and false lumen; report entry site and branch-vessel/visceral involvement. Aortic intramural haematoma = crescentic high-attenuation wall thickening WITHOUT a flap; penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer = focal ulcer through intimal plaque — the acute-aortic-syndrome triad.

Mesenteric ischaemia: SMA/coeliac embolus or thrombotic occlusion with bowel-wall hypo-/hyper-enhancement, pneumatosis or portal-venous gas — emergent; distinguish acute embolic from chronic mesenteric ischaemia (ostial atherosclerotic disease of ≥2 mesenteric vessels).
GI bleeding: focal intraluminal active contrast extravasation on the arterial phase (increasing on delayed/venous) — localise upper vs lower tract; angiodysplasia and GIST are structural sources.
Post-EVAR endoleak: contrast within the aneurysm sac outside the graft — classify by source when described; distinguish from pseudoaneurysm (contained rupture, narrow neck) and true aneurysm.
Renal artery stenosis: ostial/proximal atherosclerotic narrowing vs mid-vessel 'string-of-beads' fibromuscular dysplasia; report visceral/splenic/renal artery aneurysm and calibre.

Venous entrapment syndromes are high-yield on abdominal CTA: May-Thurner (left common iliac vein compression by right common iliac artery) and nutcracker (left renal vein compression between SMA and aorta).
Pitfall: do not over-call luminal irregularity from atherosclerotic plaque as dissection or pseudoaneurysm.

23.title: CTA Chest / PE / Aorta
23.contrast_note: Arterial-phase CTA, bolus-timed to the pulmonary arteries (PE protocol) or the thoracic aorta (dissection protocol), often ECG-gated. Intraluminal filling defects, intimal flap/false lumen, intramural haematoma, penetrating ulcer, endoleak, pseudoaneurysm and vessel-wall/plaque disease are callable; venous-phase-only and unenhanced-only high-density findings are less reliable on this timing.
hints: PE is the primary call: intraluminal 'filling defect', 'saddle embolus', segmental/subsegmental clot → 'Pulmonary Embolism'; assess RV strain (RV:LV >1, septal bowing, reflux into IVC/azygos) → 'Right heart strain'/'Submassive pulmonary embolism'. Pitfall — flow-related mixing artifact and 'In situ pulmonary artery thrombosis' over-called as embolism.

Acute aorta: intimal flap with true/false lumen → 'Aortic dissection'; hyperdense crescentic wall → 'Aortic intramural haematoma'; focal outpouching through plaque → 'Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer'; contained rupture → 'Pseudoaneurysm'.
Aortic calibre/morphology: 'Thoracic aortic dilatation', 'Thoracic aortic aneurysm', 'Ascending aortic aneurysm', 'Aortic root dilatation', 'Annuloaortic ectasia'.
Post-repair: 'Endoleak' after EVAR/TEVAR — persistent contrast within the sac; note the graft.
Pulmonary vascular/hypertension: 'Pulmonary trunk dilatation', 'Pulmonary arterial ectasia', 'Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension' (webs/eccentric wall-adherent thrombus, mosaic perfusion).
Great-vessel anomalies/variants incidentally seen: 'Aberrant right subclavian artery', 'Kommerell diverticulum', 'Left-sided superior vena cava', 'Azygos continuation of the inferior vena cava'.
Common phrasings: 'intimal flap', 'true and false lumen', 'filling defect', 'RV:LV ratio', 'saddle embolus', 'crescentic mural hyperdensity', 'contrast outside the graft'.

24.title: CTA Extremity Runoff
24.contrast_note: CTA Extremity Runoff is ARTERIAL-phase contrast of the aortoiliac and lower-extremity arteries — stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm, embolus, active extravasation, and anatomical variants (persistent sciatic artery, popliteal entrapment) are conspicuous. Venous structures are not opacified on a pure arterial runoff, so venous thrombosis is largely occult and should be flagged only when a vein is clearly expanded/non-opacified.
hints: Characterise disease as stenosis vs occlusion and length: 'short-segment occlusion with distal reconstitution', 'diffuse atherosclerotic stenoses', 'single-vessel tibial runoff'.
Aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche): distal aortic/bilateral iliac occlusion with collateralisation.
Acute limb ischaemia: abrupt intraluminal filling defect / vessel cut-off — embolus (often at bifurcations, minimal background disease) vs in-situ thrombosis (diffuse atheroma).
Aneurysm patterns: popliteal true aneurysm is frequently bilateral and thrombus-lined (embolic source); pseudoaneurysm follows trauma or access puncture — saccular outpouching with neck.

Arteriovenous malformation / AV fistula: the tell is abnormal EARLY/asymmetric venous opacification during the arterial phase (nidus, enlarged tortuous feeding artery, early draining vein) — high-flow congenital or post-traumatic/iatrogenic; this early venous filling is the deliberate exception to the 'venous structures are occult on arterial runoff' caveat.
Anatomical variants: persistent sciatic artery (enlarged continuation of the internal iliac, hypoplastic SFA) and popliteal artery entrapment (medial deviation / dynamic compression).
Pitfall: dense mural calcification, stent blooming, or motion can mimic occlusion — confirm with distal reconstitution and true axial lumen before calling occlusion.
Report the limitation explicitly when venous or delayed phases are absent; do not assert Venous thrombosis off an arterial-only acquisition.

25.title: CTA Head
25.contrast_note: Arterial-phase intracranial CTA (± neck run-off). Luminal pathology is conspicuous — saccular and basilar aneurysm, large/medium vessel occlusion, intracranial stenosis/atherosclerosis, AVM nidus, dolichoectasia, arterial fenestration and anatomical variants. Parenchymal acute blood and bone detail are better on the paired non-contrast series, and Ischaemic penumbra requires CT perfusion — do NOT assert it from CTA alone.
hints: Intraluminal filling defect or abrupt vessel cut-off at the ICA terminus / M1 -> Large vessel or Middle cerebral artery occlusion; distal branch cut-off -> Medium vessel occlusion.

Focal outpouching at a circle-of-Willis branch point (AComm, PComm, MCA bifurcation, basilar tip) -> Saccular / Basilar artery aneurysm; irregular, lobulated or with adjacent SAH -> Ruptured saccular aneurysm.
Tangle of vessels with enlarged feeding arteries and early draining vein = Brain arteriovenous malformation nidus; a Developmental Venous Anomaly has caput medusae and NO nidus.
Uniform ectatic tortuous vessel -> Dolichoectasia; focal wall bulge remote from a bifurcation may be a Pseudoaneurysm; irregular beaded lumen -> Vasculitis / Fibromuscular dysplasia.
Post-SAH CTA: hunt the culprit aneurysm and look for segmental arterial narrowing (vasospasm).
Pitfall: dense carotid-siphon calcification blooming and motion mimic stenosis/occlusion — do not over-call occlusion where calcium blooms.
Second-look the emergent leaves: Ruptured saccular aneurysm, Large vessel / Middle cerebral artery occlusion, Subarachnoid haemorrhage, AVM.

26.title: CTA Head and Neck
26.contrast_note: ARTERIAL-phase contrast, arch-to-vertex; enhancement- and lumen-dependent calls ARE valid — stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm, dissection, plaque/vulnerable plaque, tortuosity and vascular variants are all conspicuous. Caveat: this is a luminal CTA, not a perfusion or delayed study — infarct core/penumbra require the paired NCCT/CTP, and venous structures are only faintly opacified.
hints: Emergent stroke read: large-vessel / MCA / basilar occlusion — 'M1 cut-off', 'ICA terminus', 'filling defect', 'abrupt occlusion'; map to the specific occlusion leaf and second-look it first.

Carotid disease: quantify stenosis (NASCET %), note 'vulnerable/ulcerated plaque', 'carotid web', 'near-occlusion'; intracranial atherosclerosis and arterial calcification are the chronic counterparts.
Aneurysm phrasing: 'saccular aneurysm', 'outpouching', location (AComm, MCA bifurcation, basilar tip); flag any 'irregular/ruptured' contour — ruptured saccular aneurysm is emergent.

Cervical (carotid/vertebral) artery dissection is the signature emergent CTA H&N call: 'intimal flap', 'tapered/flame-shaped narrowing', 'crescentic mural thrombus/haematoma', 'pseudoaneurysm' — second-look it first alongside LVO.

Wall/variant entities: fibromuscular dysplasia ('string-of-beads'), dolichoectasia/ectasia, fenestration, persistent trigeminal/hypoglossal artery, vertebral loop/hypoplasia — do not read hypoplasia as occlusion.

Subclavian steal substrate: CTA shows the proximal subclavian/brachiocephalic stenosis-or-occlusion substrate, but the 'steal' itself is a flow-reversal (retrograde vertebral) physiology needing Doppler/MRA — only call 'Subclavian steal syndrome' if the report explicitly states flow reversal.
Neck FOV is real estate: thyroid nodule/goitre, parathyroid adenoma, cervical nodal metastasis and cervical-spine fracture/injury are reportable and often missed on a 'vascular' read.
PITFALL: penumbra/infarct-core and watershed infarct are perfusion/parenchymal calls — do not assert them from CTA lumen alone; hedge to uncertain unless the paired NCCT/CTP states them.
Vasculitis / large-vessel vasculitis: circumferential wall thickening/stenosis in a young or inflammatory context.

SAH is fundamentally an NCCT call — on the post-contrast CTA acquisition, subarachnoid contrast can mimic or obscure acute blood; only assert subarachnoid haemorrhage off the paired non-contrast series a stroke protocol includes, and hedge otherwise.

27.title: CTA Neck
27.contrast_note: Arterial-phase CTA of the neck vessels: carotid/vertebral/subclavian stenosis, plaque morphology (calcified vs soft/vulnerable), aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm, occlusion/embolism, carotid web, large-vessel vasculitic wall thickening, and arch/subclavian variants (dysphagia lusoria, subclavian steal substrate) are the primary callable findings. Soft-tissue, nodal, and delayed-enhancement processes are secondary at arterial timing. Venous-timing findings — notably 'Brachiocephalic vein stenosis' — are poorly assessable on a single arterial-phase acquisition where the veins are incompletely opacified; keep venous leaves uncertain unless the report explicitly states them.
hints: Carotid / vertebral artery stenosis — grade severity (NASCET), state calcified vs soft plaque; vulnerable plaque = thin/ruptured fibrous cap, ulceration, intraplaque haemorrhage, lipid-rich core.
Carotid web — shelf-like intraluminal filling defect at the posterior carotid bulb; cause of young/cryptogenic stroke.

Subclavian steal — proximal subclavian stenosis/occlusion proximal to the vertebral origin is the anatomic CTA substrate; the retrograde vertebral flow that DEFINES steal is a haemodynamic diagnosis inferred and typically confirmed on Doppler/4D-flow, not shown by single-phase arterial CTA. Keep 'Subclavian steal syndrome' uncertain unless the report states the flow reversal.
Dysphagia lusoria — aberrant right subclavian artery arising distal to the left subclavian, coursing retro-oesophageal.
Large-vessel vasculitis — smooth circumferential mural thickening/enhancement (Takayasu, GCA) of carotid/subclavian/vertebral walls.
Aneurysm / pseudoaneurysm / embolism / occlusion — emergent luminal findings; a pseudoaneurysm implies wall injury (trauma, dissection, mycotic).
Pitfall: carotid/vertebral tortuosity, vertebral artery loop, and vertebral artery ectasia are anatomic variants — do not report them as stenosis or aneurysm.

28.title: Coronary CTA / Calcium Score
28.contrast_note: A contrast-enhanced ECG-gated Coronary CTA renders the coronary lumen, so stenosis grade, soft/vulnerable plaque, anomalous course, myocardial bridging, and bypass grafts are all callable; a NON-CONTRAST calcium-score acquisition scores calcification ONLY — on a calcium-score series do not label luminal stenosis, soft/thin-cap plaque, or any enhancement-dependent diagnosis (myocardial infarction/ischaemia, fistulae). The thoracic aorta and pulmonary trunk in the field are assessable for calibre and calcification.
hints: CAD / stenosis: grade luminal narrowing (CAD-RADS framing) — 'non-obstructive plaque', 'high-grade LAD stenosis'; Coronary artery calcification (Agatston) is the calcium-score endpoint and maps distinct from luminal Coronary artery disease.

High-risk plaque features: low-attenuation core, positive remodelling, napkin-ring sign, spotty calcification — these support Vulnerable plaque / Thin-cap fibroatheroma; do not over-call from calcium blooming alone.

Coronary anomalies: anomalous origin with an INTERARTERIAL course (between aorta and pulmonary trunk) is the malignant, sudden-death variant — call the specific interarterial-course leaf; myocardial bridging = systolic compression of a tunnelled LAD segment.

Aorta: measure root/ascending calibre — annuloaortic ectasia, ascending aneurysm/dilatation, and aortic intramural haematoma are emergent. IMH is a crescentic HYPERDENSE wall on the non-contrast/calcium-score series, but on the contrast CTA it is a crescentic NON-ENHANCING (relatively LOW-density) wall thickening against the opacified lumen — it is often best seen on the non-contrast component, so do not exclude it just because the contrast series shows no bright crescent. Porcelain aorta is circumferential calcification.

Benign mimics: lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum spares the fossa ovalis (dumbbell fat — NOT a tumour); caseous mitral annular calcification is a benign mass mimic — do not call Secondary malignant cardiac tumour.

Left atrial appendage filling defect on an arterial-phase gated CTA is frequently incomplete-mixing artefact — hedge it as uncertain unless a delayed-phase acquisition confirms a persistent filling defect or the defect is clearly low-attenuation (true thrombus).
Incidental thoracic: pericardial effusion, centrilobular emphysema, and pneumothorax (post-procedure) are reportable in the field — check the lung/pleura reconstruction.
Pitfall: motion artefact and calcium blooming over-estimate stenosis; on a calcium-score-only study restrict output to calcifications and morphology, not luminal grades.

29.title: Dental Cone-Beam CT
29.contrast_note: NON-CONTRAST, high-resolution LIMITED-FOV dentoalveolar/maxillofacial acquisition; tooth and bone detail only, essentially no soft-tissue contrast. Confine calls to the maxillomandibular FOV — no vascular, intracranial, or soft-tissue-mass diagnoses, and no enhancement.
hints: Bread-and-butter: impacted teeth (esp. third molars) with proximity to the mandibular canal, periapical granuloma / periapical lucency, dentigerous cyst (pericoronal, around an unerupted crown), pericoronitis.

Maxillary sinus floor: odontogenic sinusitis and paranasal sinus retention cyst tracked to a dental source; periodontal ligament widening and periapical cemento-osseous dysplasia are the periapical spectrum.
TMJ: osteoarthritic change (flattening/osteophyte/erosion), dislocation; tori (mandibular/maxillary) and Stafne bone cavity are benign anatomic pickups.
MRONJ: exposed/necrotic bone, sequestration, non-healing socket in a bisphosphonate/antiresorptive context — treat as the key not-to-miss.
PITFALL — lesion character: distinguish periapical granuloma from a true cyst, and do not upgrade a benign retention cyst to sinusitis; a well-corticated pericoronal lucency is a dentigerous cyst.
Second-look for aggressive/traumatic bone: mandibular fracture and MRONJ on an otherwise routine dental study.
